query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor carbon microalloying of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 during melting, to induce an in‐situ dispersion of fine carbide precipitates along the grain boundaries, will improve its mechanical integrity (by increasing fracture toughness and compressive strength) without reducing its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibiting excellent field‐induced caloric effects but poor structural integrity (e.g., a tendency to crack under load).
generation.intervention: Introduce a low (e.g., ~0.5–1 at.%) carbon content during alloy processing so that, during solidification and subsequent thermal treatment, nano‐scale carbide precipitates form at the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under the same applied-field and pressure-field regimes and operating temperatures where the caloric performance is measured, and using standard compressive loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The in‐situ formed fine carbide precipitates will refine the grain-boundary structure and act as crack arresters, thereby reducing stress concentrations that lead to cracking.
generation.mechanism: The carbide particles impede crack propagation by blocking or deflecting growing cracks, while the overall high-entropy matrix remains unchanged so that the caloric transition (field-induced entropy change) is preserved.
generation.predicted_outcome: An alloy modified with carbon will show a noticeable increase in compressive strength and toughness (for example, improved fracture integrity, with strength increases on the order of tens of percent) while maintaining nearly the same caloric response (variations within about 10% of the baseline performance).
generation.baseline: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 without any additional alloying is highly caloric but prone to cracking under mechanical loads.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields and temperature ranges used for caloric applications, and during typical compressive loading rates; the approach must avoid the use of rare-earth elements.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal carbon concentration and processing conditions for achieving a uniform dispersion of nanoscale carbides require careful optimization; there is some uncertainty regarding whether even minor interface chemistry changes might slightly alter the caloric effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 processed with a defined minor carbon addition (targeting nano-scale carbide precipitation) and one unmodified control. Characterize both sets by TEM/SEM to assess carbide dispersion and grain size, then perform mechanical tests (compressive strength, fracture toughness) and measure the caloric response (entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) under identical applied-field/pressure conditions.
measurements: Microstructural analysis using TEM/SEM to document carbide precipitate size, distribution, and grain-boundary characteristics
Mechanical testing (compressive tests, fracture toughness measurements)
Caloric performance testing (e.g., measurement of entropy change and adiabatic temperature change under applied field and pressure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-added samples do not show a significant improvement in mechanical integrity (i.e., no statistically meaningful increase in yield strength/fracture toughness) or if the caloric response decreases by more than about 10% relative to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.
